overview.text: The Washington Post is an American newspaper founded by Stilson Hutchins in Washington, D.C.; its first issue appeared December 6, 1877. Its own founding principles emphasize telling the truth and reporting important affairs in America and around the world. The paper is especially associated with investigative journalism: it published excerpts from the Pentagon Papers in 1971, then covered the Watergate break-in and evidence linking Nixon campaign officials to secret political activity. The Watergate investigation earned The Post the 1973 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service. These episodes distinguish the paper for sustained reporting on government and public affairs, and illustrate the press’s role in examining the conduct of people in power.

key_facts.text: The Post began publishing on December 6, 1877, as a four-page paper founded by Stilson Hutchins.
In 1971, The Post published excerpts from the Pentagon Papers; the Supreme Court upheld the right of the paper and other newspapers to publish them.
The Post’s staff began covering Watergate in 1972; the newspaper received the 1973 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service for its Watergate investigation.
An early Watergate report by Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein identified one of the people arrested in the break-in as a salaried security coordinator for Nixon’s reelection committee.
The Pulitzer award recognized The Washington Post as a newspaper for the Watergate investigation, rather than awarding the prize to the reporters individually.
